bar.rule: the best frontier row held to one answer (bench/ladder.mjs frontierRowOf); met when the longest clock's solved percent reaches its score on every scored task and on the clean ones

development.what: the ARC-AGI-1 training split: the vocabulary of capability/grid-dsl.mjs was written against it

heldOut.what: the ARC-AGI-1 evaluation split, every task scored; nothing in capability/grid-dsl.mjs was tuned on it (this bench header)

split.contaminated: 1 of the 400 scored evaluation tasks shares a pair with a development task (070dd51e is pair for pair identical to training 40853293), so its score is in sample; the other scored tasks share no train or test pair with the development tasks

decidedFrom.what: every train and test pair of each scored task compared, by the sha256 of its input and output grids, with every train and test pair of the development tasks

selection.what: every task of the ARC-AGI-1 evaluation split

heldFixed: the depth (4) and the vocabulary (196 words and learners, capability/grid-dsl.mjs unchanged) are held fixed on this board; only the clock and the attempts move
secondAttemptRule: Two attempts per task, ARC's own rule: a task is right when every test input is answered right by either attempt. The search takes programs that fit every train pair (checked through grid.dsl.match cells) in the order it finds them and stops at two; a program counts as a new attempt only when its test outputs differ from every earlier attempt on at least one test input. So the two attempts are the first two programs found whose test outputs differ, and when only one such answer is found before the clock ends attempt 2 is empty. The two are listed by program length (base words, a learned last step counted as one, a macro as the words it stands for), then by discovery order (capability/grid-search.mjs orderAttempts); solvedFirst stays the program found first, which is the answer a one attempt run gives, so no task a one attempt run solves can be lost by the order.
price: PRICE: 400 tasks at 30000 ms, 2 attempts, 12 workers: 353 priced at the whole 30000 ms clock (at the 3000 ms point they ran to the clock or stopped with fewer than 2 answers), 47 at their wall there (they finished early and will again); 10647.46 task seconds, about 14.79 minutes of wall over 12 workers (plus up to 4000 ms grace on a task killed at the hard deadline); a CPU price: lanes the memory rule holds idle are not in it

memoryRule.what: a lane starts a task only under admitMb of process memory and rampMs (at most a twentieth of the clock) after the last start (or when nothing runs); over preemptMb the task started last is stopped and run again from its start later (at most maxPreempts times); a preempted run writes no row, so every row is one whole run at the whole clock; each worker has a heapMb old generation limit

control.what: the same bench on the TRAINING split (in sample: the vocabulary was written against it), a fixed seed draw of 100 tasks: mulberry32 seed 33, a Fisher Yates shuffle of the sorted ids, the first 100, sorted

published.system: Icecuber (Kaggle, program search over a hand written DSL, no LLM)

statement: On the ARC-AGI-1 evaluation split (400 of 400 tasks) the grid program search, no model, depth 4 and the same 196 word vocabulary throughout, solved: 85 of 400 (21.25 percent) at 3000 ms with 1 attempt, then 86 of 400 (21.5 percent) at 3000 ms with 2 attempts, then 91 of 400 (22.75 percent) at 30000 ms with 2 attempts. At the longest clock 272 tasks still ran out of clock, 35 found programs that fit every train pair and missed a test output, 2 exhausted the vocabulary. Paired by task id with 3000 ms, 1 attempt, the 3000 ms point with 2 attempts gained 1 and lost 0; Paired by task id with 3000 ms, 2 attempts, the 30000 ms point with 2 attempts gained 6 and lost 1. The clock bought 5 solved tasks per tenfold of clock from 3000 to 30000 ms. Contaminated, decided from data: 1 of the 400 scored evaluation tasks shares a pair with a development task (070dd51e is pair for pair identical to training 40853293), so its score is in sample; the other scored tasks share no train or test pair with the development tasks; on the 399 clean tasks the longest clock solved 90 (22.56 percent). The published no-model row is Icecuber (Kaggle, program search over a hand written DSL, no LLM) at 17 percent. The control, the same clocks on a fixed seed draw of the training split, printed 37 of 100 at 3000 ms with 1 attempt, 41 of 100 at 3000 ms with 2 attempts, 44 of 100 at 30000 ms with 2 attempts. The bar is Gemini 3.1 Pro (Preview) at 98 percent (copied from bench/verdicts/public-arc.json), and it is NOT MET. Latencies were measured on a machine shared with other builders.
